typo_or_misspelling.instructions: Does the line contain a misspelled word, typo, or malapropism (a real word used in place of the intended word)?

criteria.true: A word is misspelled, has swapped/missing/extra letters, or is a real English word that does not fit the context (e.g. "defiantly" instead of "definitely", "compliment" instead of "complement").
criteria.false: All words are spelled correctly and used with their intended meaning.

passive_voice_overuse.instructions: Is the line written in passive voice where an active construction with a named subject would be clearer?

criteria.true: The sentence hides the actor behind a passive construction ("was implemented", "has been decided") and naming the actor would make the sentence more direct.
criteria.false: The passive is justified because the actor is unknown, irrelevant, or the object deserves emphasis.

comma_splice.instructions: Does the line join two independent clauses with only a comma and no coordinating conjunction?

criteria.true: Two complete sentences are spliced together with a comma where a period, semicolon, or conjunction is needed (e.g. "The build failed, we rolled back").
criteria.false: The comma correctly separates a dependent clause, list items, or is followed by a conjunction.

dangling_modifier.instructions: Does the line contain a participial or prepositional modifier that grammatically attaches to the wrong noun — i.e. the subject of the main clause is not the one performing the action in the modifier?

criteria.true: The modifier dangles: "Running the tests, the bug was found" (the bug didn't run the tests).
criteria.false: The modifier correctly attaches to the subject of the main clause.

run_on_sentence.instructions: Is the line a run-on sentence — two or more independent clauses fused without any punctuation or conjunction between them?

criteria.true: Independent clauses run together with no separator ("The server crashed the team investigated").
criteria.false: Clauses are properly joined by punctuation, a conjunction, or the sentence has only one independent clause.

subject_verb_disagreement.instructions: Does the line contain a subject-verb agreement error where the verb's number (singular/plural) does not match its subject?

criteria.true: The verb disagrees with its subject ("The list of features are" instead of "is"; "Data show" when used as a mass noun with singular intent).
criteria.false: Subject and verb agree in number.

wrong_homophone.instructions: Does the line use a wrong homophone or commonly confused word — e.g. its/it's, their/there/they're, your/you're, affect/effect, then/than, lose/loose, lead/led?

criteria.true: A word is used that sounds like the correct word but has a different meaning or spelling.
criteria.false: All homophones and commonly confused words are used correctly.

noun_pile_up.instructions: Does the line stack three or more nouns or noun-adjective modifiers in front of a head noun, making the phrase hard to parse (e.g. "enterprise customer onboarding flow optimization metrics")?

criteria.true: A noun pile-up forces the reader to unpack which nouns modify which — splitting into a prepositional phrase would be clearer.
criteria.false: Compound nouns are short, established, or immediately clear.
